A systematic review3 of studies that compared theo- phylline with long-acting beta2 agonists found that they were both effective for control of nocturnal asthma, but that long-act- ing beta2 agonists may be more effective in reducing asthma symptoms, including night waking and the need for rescue med- ication, and are associated with fewer adverse effects. The use of xanthines in acute asthma attacks is more controver- sial. UK guidelines permit the use of intravenous aminophylline in patients with severe or life-threatening acute asthma unrespon- 1148 Bronchodilators and Anti-asthma Drugs sive to maximal doses of bronchodilators and oral corticoster- oids, (a point supported in children4 but not in adults5 by system- atic review) whereas US guidelines do not consider xanthines have any benefit over the optimal use of beta agonists and conse- quently do not recommend their use (see p.1108). 1.
